from __future__ import annotations

from typing import Dict, Iterable, List, Sequence, Set, Tuple

Edge = Tuple[int, int]
Triangle = Tuple[int, int, int]


def is_rips_edge(cloud: Sequence[float], eps: float, edge: Edge) -> bool:
    """(a,b) with a < b is an edge of the scale-eps complex iff |x_a - x_b| <= eps."""
    a, b = edge
    return a < b and abs(cloud[a] - cloud[b]) <= eps


def degrees(chain: Iterable[Edge]) -> Dict[int, int]:
    """Vertex degrees of an F_2 one-chain."""
    deg: Dict[int, int] = {}
    for a, b in chain:
        deg[a] = deg.get(a, 0) + 1
        deg[b] = deg.get(b, 0) + 1
    return deg


def is_cycle(chain: Set[Edge]) -> bool:
    """Over F_2 the boundary of a chain is its set of odd-degree vertices."""
    return all(d % 2 == 0 for d in degrees(chain).values())


def weight(chain: Iterable[Edge]) -> int:
    """The termination measure mu(E) = sum of the right endpoints of the edges of E."""
    return sum(b for _a, b in chain)


def reduce_cycle_to_triangles(cloud: Sequence[float], eps: float,
                              cycle: Set[Edge]) -> List[Triangle]:
    """
    Write an F_2 one-cycle of a line Rips complex as a sum of Rips triangles.

    Invariant: the working chain is always a cycle of Rips edges.  Each iteration takes
    the maximal vertex v carried by the chain; its degree is even and nonzero, so two
    edges (u,v) and (w,v) with u < w < v are present.  Since x_u and x_w both lie in the
    window [x_v - eps, x_v], the chord (u,w) is a Rips edge, so T = {(u,w),(w,v),(u,v)}
    is a Rips triangle.  Adding T keeps all degrees even and strictly lowers mu, because
    two edges of weight v disappear and at most one of weight w < v appears.  Hence the
    loop performs at most mu(cycle) iterations and returns a decomposition certifying
    that the cycle bounds -- a constructive proof that H_1 vanishes at every scale.
    """
    triangles: List[Triangle] = []
    work: Set[Edge] = set(cycle)
    if not all(is_rips_edge(cloud, eps, e) for e in work):
        raise ValueError("input chain must consist of Rips edges at this scale")
    if not is_cycle(work):
        raise ValueError("input chain must be a cycle (all degrees even)")
    while work:
        v = max(b for _a, b in work)
        left = sorted(a for (a, b) in work if b == v)
        u, w = left[0], left[1]
        triangle: Set[Edge] = {(u, w), (w, v), (u, v)}
        before = weight(work)
        work ^= triangle
        assert weight(work) < before
        triangles.append((u, w, v))
    return triangles

  <p>Every jump of the staircase sits at an <strong>even</strong> integer (with the single

// ------------------------------------------------------------------ histogram
const hist = document.getElementById('hist'), hctx = hist.getContext('2d');
const HMAX = 44;

  hctx.fillStyle='#22456b'; hctx.font='13px Georgia,serif';

                MEANLEN.toFixed(2), m.l+6, m.t+12);
}
hist.addEventListener('mousemove', ev=>{

<div class="wrap">
  <h1>Pull the Loop to the Left: why a point cloud on a line has no holes</h1>
  <p class="lede">A one-dimensional hole in a point cloud is a loop of points, each within
  ε of the next, that is not filled in by triangles. This widget lets you build a
  loop out of primes and then watch it die. At every step the algorithm looks at the
  <strong>rightmost</strong> point of the loop, notices that its two loop-neighbours must
  see each other (they both sit inside a window of width ε to the left of it), and
  cancels the triangle they span. The loop is dragged leftwards until nothing remains.
  Since this always works, the first homology of a line point cloud vanishes at
  <em>every</em> scale — there is no room on a line for a hole.</p>

  <div class="panel">
    <div class="row">

      the first point). Edges longer than ε are rejected. Then press
      <em>reduce one step</em>.</p>

      <div class="stat"><div class="k">is a cycle? (all degrees even)</div><div class="v" id="cyc">–</div></div>

  <details>
    <summary>Click to reveal the formal statement and its proof</summary>
    <p><strong>Vanishing Theorem.</strong> Let <em>x</em><sub>0</sub> < <em>x</em><sub>1</sub> < …
    be points on the real line and fix a scale ε. Regard a one-chain with
    coefficients mod 2 as a finite set <em>E</em> of edges (<em>a</em>,<em>b</em>),
    <em>a</em> < <em>b</em>, with |<em>x<sub>a</sub></em> − <em>x<sub>b</sub></em>| ≤ ε;
    addition of chains is symmetric difference, and <em>E</em> is a <em>cycle</em> when
    every vertex has even degree. Then every cycle is a sum of triangles of the complex,
    so <em>H</em><sub>1</sub> = 0.</p>
    <p><strong>Proof.</strong> Give the chain the weight
    μ(<em>E</em>) = ∑<sub>(a,b)∈E</sub> <em>b</em>, and induct on μ. If
    <em>E</em> is empty we are done. Otherwise let <em>v</em> be the largest right endpoint
    occurring in <em>E</em>; every edge at <em>v</em> has <em>v</em> on its right, and the
    degree of <em>v</em> is even and nonzero, hence at least 2: two edges
    (<em>u</em>,<em>v</em>) and (<em>w</em>,<em>v</em>) are present, say with
    <em>u</em> < <em>w</em> < <em>v</em>. Since
    <em>x<sub>v</sub></em> − <em>x<sub>u</sub></em> ≤ ε and
    <em>x<sub>u</sub></em> < <em>x<sub>w</sub></em> < <em>x<sub>v</sub></em>, the chord
    (<em>u</em>,<em>w</em>) is also an edge, so
    <em>T</em> = {(<em>u</em>,<em>w</em>), (<em>w</em>,<em>v</em>), (<em>u</em>,<em>v</em>)}
    is a triangle of the complex. Every vertex has degree 0 or 2 in <em>T</em>, so
    <em>T</em> + <em>E</em> is again a cycle; and its weight is strictly smaller, because
    two edges of weight <em>v</em> are removed while at most one of weight
    <em>w</em> < <em>v</em> appears. By induction <em>T</em> + <em>E</em> is a sum of
    triangles, hence so is <em>E</em> = <em>T</em> + (<em>T</em> + <em>E</em>). □</p>
    <p>The counter above is the weight μ: watch it drop monotonically. That monotone
    quantity is exactly what makes the "pull to the left" move terminate; an induction on
    the number of edges would fail, because the edge count can stay the same.</p>
  </details>

  <details>
    <summary>Why this kills the conjectured "twin prime hole"</summary>
    <p>It was tempting to guess that the primes carry a long-lived one-dimensional feature
    born at ε = 2, the twin-prime scale, and that its persistence encodes the Twin
    Prime Conjecture. The theorem above rules this out at every scale and for every point
    cloud on a line: the primes have no holes whatsoever. What is true is one dimension
    lower. The number of components that merge as the scale crosses 2 — the single
    step <em>b</em><sub>0</sub>(1) − <em>b</em><sub>0</sub>(2) of the component
    staircase — counts exactly the twin pairs, and the Twin Prime Conjecture says
    precisely that this step is unbounded as more primes are included.</p>
  </details>

### A guided tour of the persistent homology of the prime numbers

Lay the primes $2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, \dots$ on a ruler. You get a *point cloud*: a scatter of dots on the real line, thinning out as you walk right, with no obvious rhythm. Modern data analysis has a standard way of interrogating a point cloud — **persistent homology** — and it asks two questions: *at what resolution does this data look connected?* and *at what resolution does it have holes?*

This page is a tour of what happens when you ask those questions of the primes. The answer turns out to overturn the most natural guess and replace it with something sharper.

---

## 1. The dial

Fix a scale $\varepsilon$ and join any two primes lying within distance $\varepsilon$ of each other. The resulting object is the **Vietoris–Rips complex** $R_\varepsilon$. At $\varepsilon = 0$ every prime is its own island. As you raise $\varepsilon$, islands merge. Recording the scale at which each island disappears produces the **barcode**, and counting islands as a function of $\varepsilon$ produces the **Betti curve**
$$b_0(\varepsilon, n) = \#\{\text{$\varepsilon$-connected components among the first } n+1 \text{ primes}\}.$$

Turn the dial yourself. Watch which primes fuse first, watch the twin pairs snap together at $\varepsilon = 2$, and notice — this is the first surprise — that **absolutely nothing ever happens at an odd scale**.

{{interactive_demo:0}}

<details>
<summary>Why the barcode of a line is just the list of gaps</summary>

On a line, a run of consecutive primes is $\varepsilon$-connected exactly when every gap inside the run is at most $\varepsilon$. (One direction: any $\varepsilon$-hop across an intermediate consecutive pair bounds that pair's gap. The other: if all internal gaps are small, walk left to right.) So the components at scale $\varepsilon$ are precisely the runs cut apart by the gaps exceeding $\varepsilon$, giving

$$b_0(\varepsilon, n) = 1 + \#\{\, i < n : g_i > \varepsilon \,\}, \qquad g_i = p_{i+1} - p_i,$$

and the $i$-th finite bar of the barcode is the interval $[0, g_i)$. In dimension zero, *the topology of the primes is the arithmetic of prime gaps* — nothing more and nothing less.
</details>

---

## 2. The guess, and why it fails

Near $x$ the primes have average spacing $\log x$ — this is the [Prime Number Theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_number_theorem). A random set with that spacing is a [Poisson process](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poisson_point_process), whose component bars have lengths that are **exponentially distributed** with mean $\log x$. So the natural conjecture is: the prime barcode looks exponential.

It cannot, and the reason is one line of arithmetic.

> **Quantisation Theorem.** The first bar of the prime barcode has length exactly $1$ (from $2$ to $3$). Every other bar has even length $2k$ with $k \ge 1$.

Every prime past $2$ is odd; the difference of two odd numbers is even. Therefore the bar-length measure is **atomic**, supported on $\{1\} \cup \{2, 4, 6, \dots\}$, whereas an exponential law is absolutely continuous and puts mass
$$e^{-2k/m} - e^{-(2k+2)/m} > 0$$
into every window $(2k, 2k+2)$, for every mean $m > 0$. The primes put exactly zero bars there — not few, *zero*, at every truncation, forever. Hover the windows in the chart above to compare.

The refutation is also **robust**: every prime bar length is at distance at least $1$ from every odd integer $\ge 3$, so perturbing the whole barcode by less than $1/2$ in the bottleneck metric leaves the empty windows empty.

And it is not just the shape of the distribution that fails, but the tail. Look at $m! + 2, m! + 3, \dots, m! + m$: the $j$-th is divisible by $j$, so all of them are composite. That is a prime-free stretch of length $m-1$ placed at will, so:

> **Unbounded Bars.** For every $N$ some bar of the prime barcode has length at least $N$. No single scale $\log x$ governs the barcode.

{{visualization:0}}

---

## 3. Reading the staircase

Because every gap past the first is even, the Betti curve is **constant on every interval $[2k, 2k+2)$**: it is a staircase whose treads sit between consecutive even integers. Running the staircase backwards recovers the gap histogram exactly:

> **Inversion Formula.** For $k \ge 1$,
> $$\#\{\, i < n : g_i = 2k \,\} \;=\; b_0(2k-1, n) - b_0(2k+1, n).$$

And integrating it forwards recovers the primes themselves:

> **Betti Area Identity.** $\displaystyle \int_0^\infty \big( b_0(\varepsilon, n) - 1 \big)\, d\varepsilon \;=\; p_n - 2.$

The proof is a layer cake: at scale $\varepsilon$ the $i$-th bar contributes $1$ to the reduced count exactly while $\varepsilon < g_i$, so it contributes area $g_i$; the gaps telescope. Divide by $n$ and you get the exact "average prime gap", $(p_n - 2)/n$ — the quantity whose asymptotics the Prime Number Theorem describes.

{{algorithm:1}}

---

## 4. Where the twin primes actually live

The conjectured picture put the [Twin Prime Conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twin_prime) in dimension one, as a long-lived hole born at $\varepsilon = 2$. In fact it lives one dimension lower, in a single step of the staircase.

Turn the dial from just under $2$ up to $2$: exactly the pairs of primes differing by $2$ merge. So the height of that one step counts twin pairs.

> **Twin Prime Reformulation.** There are infinitely many twin primes **iff** the single Betti step $b_0(1,n) - b_0(2,n)$ is unbounded as $n \to \infty$.

{{demo:1}}

---

## 5. And where the holes are not

Could the primes have a hole? A hole is a loop of points, each within $\varepsilon$ of the next, that is not filled in by triangles. On a line, the answer is a flat no — and the reason is a picture, not a computation.

Take any loop and look at its **rightmost** point $v$. Its two loop-neighbours both lie within $\varepsilon$ of $v$ and both lie to its left, so both sit inside the window $[v - \varepsilon, v]$, so they are within $\varepsilon$ of *each other*. The chord is there. Cancel the triangle it spans, and the loop shrinks. Repeat.

> **Vanishing Theorem.** For any strictly increasing point cloud on the real line and any scale $\varepsilon$, every mod-$2$ one-cycle of the scale-$\varepsilon$ complex is a sum of triangles of that complex. Hence $H_1 = 0$ at every scale: the prime point cloud has no holes, ever.

Build a loop yourself and watch it die. The quantity to keep an eye on is the **weight** $\mu(E) = \sum_{(a,b) \in E} b$, the sum of the right endpoints: it drops strictly at every step, which is exactly why the process terminates.

{{interactive_demo:1}}

{{algorithm:2}}

The theorem is not vacuous — the prime complex really does contain one-cycles. At scale $\varepsilon = 8$ the quadrilateral $3 \to 5 \to 7 \to 11 \to 3$ is a genuine nonzero cycle. It is simply the sum of the two triangles $\{3,5,7\}$ and $\{3,7,11\}$. The loop exists; the hole does not.

---

## 6. The primes repel themselves

Killing the exponential law leaves a weaker hypothesis standing: perhaps the bar lengths are at least *independent*. They are not, and the obstruction is again a congruence.

Two adjacent bars of length $2$ would mean three primes $p, p+2, p+4$. One of any three numbers spaced $2$ apart is divisible by $3$, and once $p \ge 5$ that one is composite.

> **Exclusion Theorem.** Past the very start of the barcode, if two adjacent bars have the same length $d$, then $3 \mid d$. In particular adjacent twin bars never occur — the single exception in the entire barcode is the triple $3, 5, 7$.

An independent model with $\mathbb{P}(\text{length} = 2) = q > 0$ predicts about $(n-1)q^2$ adjacent twin pairs among $n$ bars. The primes deliver zero. And the exclusion generalises to every prime modulus:

> **Block Divisibility Theorem.** For every prime $q$ and every start past $q$, some block of fewer than $q$ consecutive bars has total length divisible by $q$.

(Pigeonhole: $q$ consecutive primes all exceeding $q$ occupy only $q-1$ residue classes mod $q$, so two coincide, and the bars between them sum to a multiple of $q$.) Taking $q = 5$: no four consecutive bars of length $2$, i.e. no five primes in arithmetic progression with common difference $2$.

The picture below shows the full two-point function of the barcode. Every black cell is a proved exclusion, and every proved exclusion is a black cell.

{{visualization:1}}

---

## 7. Everything at once

The barcode is a **complete invariant**: $p_n = 2 + \sum_{m<n} g_m$. Nothing about the primes is lost in passing to their topology, which is why the barcode inherits so much rigid structure and why it can never be "generic".

Run the full numerical tour — quantisation, empty windows, the staircase and its inversion, the area identity, the twin step and its cap, the exclusion laws, and a constructive reduction of a one-cycle to triangles:

{{demo:0}}

{{algorithm:0}}

---

## What to take away

The primes do have a shape, and the shape is entirely zero-dimensional:

- **atomic** — bar lengths confined to $\{1\} \cup 2\mathbb{N}$, with hard empty windows;
- **heavy-tailed** — bars of arbitrarily large length, so no single scale governs it;
- **correlated** — adjacent equal bars forbidden unless $3$ divides the length, with an analogous law at every prime modulus;
- **complete** — the barcode reconstructs the primes exactly;
- **calibrated** — the area under the reduced Betti curve is exactly $p_n - 2$.

The Poisson heuristic remains an excellent guide to prime behaviour *in the large*; what the topology exposes is precisely where it fails, namely at small scales, where divisibility rules. And the hardest open question in the subject sits in plain view at the very first step of the staircase: turn the dial from $1$ to $2$, count the merges, and ask whether that number grows forever. Nobody knows.

/-! ## 1. Arithmetic quantisation of the `H₀` barcode -/

/-- Consecutive primes are strictly increasing (specialisation of `Nat.nth_strictMono`). -/
theorem nth_prime_lt_succ (i : ℕ) : Nat.nth Nat.Prime i < Nat.nth Nat.Prime (i + 1) :=
  Nat.nth_strictMono (p := Nat.Prime) Nat.infinite_setOf_prime (Nat.lt_succ_self i)

/-- Monotonicity of the prime enumeration. -/
theorem nth_prime_mono {i j : ℕ} (h : i ≤ j) : Nat.nth Nat.Prime i ≤ Nat.nth Nat.Prime j :=
  Nat.nth_monotone (p := Nat.Prime) Nat.infinite_setOf_prime h

/-- The first prime after `2` is `3`. -/
theorem nth_prime_one : Nat.nth Nat.Prime 1 = 3 := by simp

/-- Every prime past the first is at least `3`. -/
theorem three_le_nth_prime {i : ℕ} (hi : 1 ≤ i) : 3 ≤ Nat.nth Nat.Prime i := by
  have h := nth_prime_mono hi
  rwa [nth_prime_one] at h

/-- Every prime past the first is odd. -/
theorem nth_prime_odd {i : ℕ} (hi : 1 ≤ i) : Odd (Nat.nth Nat.Prime i) := by
  have hp := Nat.prime_nth_prime i
  have h3 := three_le_nth_prime hi
  rcases hp.eq_two_or_odd' with h | h
  · omega
  · exact h

/-- Prime gaps, i.e. finite `H₀` bar lengths, are positive. -/
theorem primeGap_pos (i : ℕ) : 0 < primeGap i := by
  have := nth_prime_lt_succ i
  unfold primeGap
  omega

/-- The first bar of the prime barcode has length `1` (the bar `2 → 3`). -/
theorem primeGap_zero : primeGap 0 = 1 := by
  unfold primeGap
  simp

/-- **Quantisation.**  Every bar of the prime barcode past the first has even length. -/
theorem primeGap_even {i : ℕ} (hi : 1 ≤ i) : Even (primeGap i) := by
  obtain ⟨a, ha⟩ := nth_prime_odd hi
  obtain ⟨b, hb⟩ := nth_prime_odd (i := i + 1) (by omega)
  have hlt := nth_prime_lt_succ i
  refine ⟨b - a, ?_⟩
  unfold primeGap
  omega

/-- Every bar past the first has length at least `2`. -/
theorem two_le_primeGap {i : ℕ} (hi : 1 ≤ i) : 2 ≤ primeGap i := by
  obtain ⟨a, ha⟩ := primeGap_even hi
  have hpos := primeGap_pos i
  omega

/-- Bar length `1` occurs exactly once in the whole prime barcode. -/
theorem primeGap_eq_one_iff (i : ℕ) : primeGap i = 1 ↔ i = 0 := by
  constructor
  · intro h
    by_contra hi
    have := two_le_primeGap (i := i) (by omega)
    omega
  · rintro rfl
    exact primeGap_zero

/-- **Bar-length quantisation, real form.**  The `i`-th finite `H₀` bar of the prime
cloud (`i ≥ 1`) has length exactly `2k` for some `k ≥ 1`. -/
theorem bar_length_quantized {i : ℕ} (hi : 1 ≤ i) :
    ∃ k : ℕ, 1 ≤ k ∧ P (i + 1) - P i = 2 * (k : ℝ) := by
  obtain ⟨a, ha⟩ := primeGap_even hi
  refine ⟨a, ?_, ?_⟩
  · have := two_le_primeGap hi
    omega
  · rw [death_scale_eq_primeGap, ha]
    push_cast
    ring

/-- The number of finite `H₀` bars among the first `n` whose length lies in the open
interval `(a, b)`. -/
noncomputable def barCount (n : ℕ) (a b : ℝ) : ℕ :=
  ((Finset.range n).filter (fun i => a < P (i + 1) - P i ∧ P (i + 1) - P i < b)).card

/-- **Empty even windows.**  No prime bar has length strictly between `2k` and `2k+2`

together with the single atom `1`. -/

  rw [death_scale_eq_primeGap]
  rintro ⟨-, h2⟩
  have : (1 : ℕ) ≤ primeGap i := primeGap_pos i
  have : ((1 : ℕ) : ℝ) ≤ ((primeGap i : ℕ) : ℝ) := by exact_mod_cast this
  push_cast at this
  linarith

/-- The mass an exponential law of mean `m > 0` assigns to a nondegenerate window
`(a,b)` is strictly positive. -/
theorem exp_window_mass_pos {m a b : ℝ} (hm : 0 < m) (hab : a < b) :
    0 < Real.exp (-a / m) - Real.exp (-b / m) := by
  have h : -b / m < -a / m := by gcongr
  simpa using Real.exp_lt_exp.mpr h

/-- **Refutation of the Poisson / exponential conjecture.**  For every proposed mean
`m > 0` and every even window `(2k, 2k+2)` with `k ≥ 1`, an exponential law of mean
`m` predicts a strictly positive fraction of bars inside the window, while the prime
barcode contains *no* bar there, at every truncation `n`.  Hence the `H₀` bar lengths
of the primes are not exponentially distributed for any mean — in particular not for
`m = log x`. -/
theorem poisson_exponential_model_refuted {m : ℝ} (hm : 0 < m) (n : ℕ) {k : ℕ}
    (hk : 1 ≤ k) :
    (barCount n (2 * k) (2 * k + 2) : ℝ) = 0 ∧
      0 < Real.exp (-(2 * (k : ℝ)) / m) - Real.exp (-(2 * (k : ℝ) + 2) / m) := by
  refine ⟨by rw [bar_window_count_eq_zero n hk]; norm_num, ?_⟩
  exact exp_window_mass_pos hm (by linarith)

/-- The same refutation at the bottom of the range: the model predicts a positive
fraction of bars shorter than `1`, the primes have none. -/
theorem poisson_model_refuted_short {m : ℝ} (hm : 0 < m) (n : ℕ) :
    (barCount n 0 1 : ℝ) = 0 ∧ 0 < Real.exp (-(0 : ℝ) / m) - Real.exp (-(1 : ℝ) / m) := by
  refine ⟨by rw [bar_window_count_short_eq_zero n]; norm_num, ?_⟩
  exact exp_window_mass_pos hm (by norm_num)

/-! ## 3. The Betti staircase is even-quantised -/

/-- **Even quantisation of the Betti curve.**  For `k ≥ 1` the Betti number
`b₀(ε, n)` of the prime cloud is constant for `ε ∈ [2k, 2k+2)`: every jump of the
`H₀` staircase sits at an even integer.  A Poisson cloud of any intensity has, with
probability one, a Betti curve that is nonconstant on every subinterval. -/
theorem prime_bettiZero_const_on_even_window (n : ℕ) {k : ℕ} (hk : 1 ≤ k) {e₁ e₂ : ℝ}
    (h1 : 2 * (k : ℝ) ≤ e₁) (h2 : e₁ ≤ e₂) (h3 : e₂ < 2 * (k : ℝ) + 2) :
    bettiZero P e₁ n = bettiZero P e₂ n := by
  rw [prime_bettiZero_eq, prime_bettiZero_eq]
  congr 2
  apply Finset.filter_congr
  intro i _
  constructor
  · intro h
    rcases Nat.eq_zero_or_pos i with rfl | hi
    · rw [primeGap_zero] at h
      have hk' : (1 : ℝ) ≤ (k : ℝ) := by exact_mod_cast hk
      push_cast at h
      linarith
    · obtain ⟨a, ha⟩ := primeGap_even hi
      rw [ha] at h ⊢
      have hka : k < a := by
        by_contra hc
        push_neg at hc
        have : ((a : ℕ) : ℝ) ≤ (k : ℝ) := by exact_mod_cast hc
        push_cast at h
        linarith
      have : (k : ℝ) + 1 ≤ (a : ℝ) := by exact_mod_cast hka
      push_cast
      linarith
  · intro h
    linarith

/-! ## 4. The twin prime conjecture as an unbounded Betti step -/

/-- The `ε = 2` step of the Betti staircase: the number of components that merge as
the scale crosses `2`. -/
noncomputable def twinStep (n : ℕ) : ℕ := bettiZero P 1 n - bettiZero P 2 n

/-- Recasting a real threshold on gaps as a natural-number threshold. -/
theorem filter_gap_cast (n c : ℕ) :
    (Finset.range n).filter (fun i => (c : ℝ) < (primeGap i : ℝ))
      = (Finset.range n).filter (fun i => c < primeGap i) := by
  apply Finset.filter_congr
  intro i _
  exact_mod_cast Iff.rfl

/-- Splitting the gaps exceeding `1` into those exceeding `2` and the twin gaps. -/
theorem card_gap_split (n : ℕ) :
    ((Finset.range n).filter (fun i => 1 < primeGap i)).card
      = ((Finset.range n).filter (fun i => 2 < primeGap i)).card
        + ((Finset.range n).filter (fun i => primeGap i = 2)).card := by
  rw [← Finset.card_union_of_disjoint, ← Finset.filter_or]
  · congr 1
    apply Finset.filter_congr
    intro i _
    constructor
    · intro h; omega
    · intro h; omega
  · simp only [Finset.disjoint_left, Finset.mem_filter]
    rintro a ⟨-, ha⟩ ⟨-, hb⟩
    omega

/-- The `ε = 2` Betti step counts exactly the twin pairs among the first `n` bars. -/
theorem twinStep_eq_card (n : ℕ) :
    twinStep n = ((Finset.range n).filter (fun i => primeGap i = 2)).card := by
  unfold twinStep
  rw [prime_bettiZero_eq, prime_bettiZero_eq]
  have e1 : ((1 : ℝ)) = ((1 : ℕ) : ℝ) := by norm_num
  have e2 : ((2 : ℝ)) = ((2 : ℕ) : ℝ) := by norm_num
  rw [e1, e2, filter_gap_cast, filter_gap_cast, card_gap_split]
  omega

/-- A predicate holds infinitely often iff its counting function is unbounded. -/
theorem infinite_iff_count_unbounded (S : ℕ → Prop) [DecidablePred S] :
    {i | S i}.Infinite ↔ ∀ N : ℕ, ∃ n, N ≤ ((Finset.range n).filter S).card := by
  classical
  constructor
  · intro hinf N
    obtain ⟨T, hTsub, hTcard⟩ := hinf.exists_subset_card_eq N
    refine ⟨(T.sup id) + 1, ?_⟩
    have hsub : T ⊆ (Finset.range ((T.sup id) + 1)).filter S := by
      intro x hx
      simp only [Finset.mem_filter, Finset.mem_range]
      exact ⟨Nat.lt_succ_of_le (Finset.le_sup (f := id) hx), hTsub hx⟩
    calc N = T.card := hTcard.symm
      _ ≤ _ := Finset.card_le_card hsub
  · intro h
    by_contra hfin
    rw [Set.not_infinite] at hfin
    obtain ⟨n, hn⟩ := h (hfin.toFinset.card + 1)
    have hsub : ((Finset.range n).filter S) ⊆ hfin.toFinset := by
      intro x hx
      simp only [Finset.mem_filter] at hx
      simpa using hx.2
    have := Finset.card_le_card hsub
    omega

/-- **Twin primes live in `H₀`, not in `H₁`.**  The twin prime conjecture holds if and
only if the single Betti step of the prime barcode at scale `ε = 2`,
`b₀(1,n) − b₀(2,n)`, is unbounded as the truncation `n` grows. -/
theorem twinPrime_iff_twinStep_unbounded :
    {p : ℕ | p.Prime ∧ (p + 2).Prime}.Infinite ↔ ∀ N : ℕ, ∃ n, N ≤ twinStep n := by
  rw [twinPrime_iff_infinitely_many_gap_two]
  rw [infinite_iff_count_unbounded (fun i => primeGap i = 2)]
  constructor <;> intro h N <;> obtain ⟨n, hn⟩ := h N <;> exact ⟨n, by rwa [twinStep_eq_card] at *⟩

/-! ## 5. Bars of arbitrarily large length -/

/-- Numbers of the form `m! + j` with `2 ≤ j ≤ m` are composite. -/
theorem not_prime_factorial_add {m j : ℕ} (h2 : 2 ≤ j) (hj : j ≤ m) :
    ¬ Nat.Prime (Nat.factorial m + j) := by
  intro hp
  have hdvd : j ∣ Nat.factorial m + j := Nat.dvd_add (Nat.dvd_factorial (by omega) hj) dvd_rfl
  have hfac : 0 < Nat.factorial m := Nat.factorial_pos m
  rcases hp.eq_one_or_self_of_dvd j hdvd with h | h <;> omega

/-- **Arbitrarily long bars.**  For every `N` some finite `H₀` bar of the prime cloud
has length at least `N`.  Hence the barcode has no exponential tail with a fixed mean
and, in particular, no single `log x` scale governs it. -/
theorem exists_large_primeGap (N : ℕ) : ∃ i, N ≤ primeGap i := by
  classical
  set m := N + 2 with hm
  set n := Nat.count Nat.Prime (Nat.factorial m + 2) with hn
  have hfac : 2 ≤ Nat.factorial m := by
    have h := Nat.factorial_le (m := 2) (n := m) (by omega)
    simpa [Nat.factorial] using h
  have hn1 : 1 ≤ n := by
    have h : Nat.count Nat.Prime 3 ≤ n := Nat.count_monotone _ (by omega)
    have h3 : Nat.count Nat.Prime 3 = 1 := by decide
    omega
  have hlt : Nat.nth Nat.Prime (n - 1) < Nat.factorial m + 2 :=
    Nat.nth_lt_of_lt_count (by omega)
  have hge : Nat.factorial m + 2 ≤ Nat.nth Nat.Prime n := by
    by_contra hc
    push_neg at hc
    have hp : Nat.Prime (Nat.nth Nat.Prime n) := Nat.prime_nth_prime n
    have h1 : Nat.count Nat.Prime (Nat.nth Nat.Prime n + 1) = n + 1 := by
      rw [Nat.count_succ]
      simp [hp, Nat.count_nth_of_infinite Nat.infinite_setOf_prime]
    have h2 : Nat.count Nat.Prime (Nat.nth Nat.Prime n + 1) ≤ n :=
      Nat.count_monotone _ (by omega)
    omega
  have hbig : Nat.factorial m + m + 1 ≤ Nat.nth Nat.Prime n := by
    by_contra hc
    push_neg at hc
    obtain ⟨j, hj⟩ : ∃ j, Nat.nth Nat.Prime n = Nat.factorial m + j :=
      ⟨Nat.nth Nat.Prime n - Nat.factorial m, by omega⟩
    exact not_prime_factorial_add (m := m) (j := j) (by omega) (by omega)
      (hj ▸ Nat.prime_nth_prime n)
  refine ⟨n - 1, ?_⟩
  have hsucc : n - 1 + 1 = n := by omega
  unfold primeGap
  rw [hsucc]
  omega

/-- The prime barcode is unbounded: bar lengths exceed every real bound. -/
theorem barcode_unbounded (C : ℝ) : ∃ i, C < P (i + 1) - P i := by
  obtain ⟨i, hi⟩ := exists_large_primeGap (⌈C⌉.toNat + 1)
  refine ⟨i, ?_⟩
  rw [death_scale_eq_primeGap]
  have h1 : C ≤ (⌈C⌉.toNat : ℝ) := by
    calc C ≤ (⌈C⌉ : ℝ) := Int.le_ceil C
      _ ≤ ((⌈C⌉.toNat : ℤ) : ℝ) := by exact_mod_cast Int.self_le_toNat _
      _ = (⌈C⌉.toNat : ℝ) := by push_cast; ring
  have h2 : ((⌈C⌉.toNat + 1 : ℕ) : ℝ) ≤ (primeGap i : ℝ) := by exact_mod_cast hi
  push_cast at h2
  linarith

/-! ## 6. No `H₁`: every cycle of a line Rips graph has a chord -/

/-- A `k`-periodic sequence is determined by residues mod `k`. -/
theorem periodic_mod {k : ℕ} (hk : 0 < k) {c : ℕ → ℕ} (hper : ∀ i, c (i + k) = c i)
    (i : ℕ) : c i = c (i % k) := by
  induction i using Nat.strong_induction_on with
  | _ i ih =>
    rcases lt_or_ge i k with h | h
    · rw [Nat.mod_eq_of_lt h]
    · have h1 : c i = c (i - k) := by
        have hp := hper (i - k)
        rwa [Nat.sub_add_cancel h] at hp
      have h2 : i % k = (i - k) % k := Nat.mod_eq_sub_mod h
      rw [h1, ih (i - k) (by omega), h2]

/-- **Every cycle in a line Rips graph has a two-step chord.**  If `c` is a closed
cycle of length `k ≥ 4` in the Vietoris–Rips graph of a strictly increasing point
cloud `p` at scale `ε` (periodic of period `k`, injective on one period, consecutive
vertices `ε`-close), then some pair of vertices at cyclic distance exactly `2` is
`ε`-close as well: the cycle has a genuine chord.

Geometrically: the leftmost vertex of the cycle sees both of its cycle neighbours
inside the window `[·, · + ε]`, so those two neighbours are within `ε` of each other.
Consequently the Rips graph of *any* point cloud on a line is chordal — there are no
induced cycles of length `≥ 4`, hence no minimal one-cycle that could bound a hole. -/
theorem cycle_has_two_step_chord {p : ℕ → ℝ} (hp : StrictMono p) {ε : ℝ} {k : ℕ}
    (hk : 4 ≤ k) {c : ℕ → ℕ} (hper : ∀ i, c (i + k) = c i)
    (hinj : ∀ i < k, ∀ j < k, c i = c j → i = j)
    (hadj : ∀ i, |p (c i) - p (c (i + 1))| ≤ ε) :
    ∃ t, c t ≠ c (t + 2) ∧ |p (c t) - p (c (t + 2))| ≤ ε := by
  have hk0 : 0 < k := by omega
  obtain ⟨i₀, hi₀mem, hi₀min⟩ :=
    Finset.exists_min_image (Finset.range k) c ⟨0, by simp [hk0]⟩
  simp only [Finset.mem_range] at hi₀mem
  have hmin : ∀ i, c i₀ ≤ c i := by
    intro i
    rw [periodic_mod hk0 hper i]
    exact hi₀min _ (Finset.mem_range.mpr (Nat.mod_lt _ hk0))
  set t := if i₀ = 0 then k - 1 else i₀ - 1 with ht
  have hstep : c (t + 1) = c i₀ := by
    by_cases h : i₀ = 0
    · have htk : t + 1 = k := by simp [ht, h]; omega
      rw [htk, h]
      simpa using hper 0
    · have htk : t + 1 = i₀ := by simp [ht, h]; omega
      rw [htk]
  refine ⟨t, ?_, ?_⟩
  · intro hcontra
    have h1 : c (t % k) = c ((t + 2) % k) := by
      rw [← periodic_mod hk0 hper, ← periodic_mod hk0 hper]
      exact hcontra
    have h2 : t % k = (t + 2) % k := hinj _ (Nat.mod_lt _ hk0) _ (Nat.mod_lt _ hk0) h1
    have hmod : Nat.ModEq k t (t + 2) := h2
    have hdvd : k ∣ 2 := by
      have h := (Nat.modEq_iff_dvd' (by omega : t ≤ t + 2)).mp hmod
      simpa using h
    have := Nat.le_of_dvd (by norm_num) hdvd
    omega
  · have e1 : p (c (t + 1)) ≤ p (c t) := hp.monotone (by rw [hstep]; exact hmin _)
    have e2 : p (c (t + 1)) ≤ p (c (t + 2)) := hp.monotone (by rw [hstep]; exact hmin _)
    have a1 := hadj t
    have a2 := hadj (t + 1)
    have ht2 : t + 1 + 1 = t + 2 := by omega
    rw [ht2] at a2
    rw [abs_le] at a1 a2 ⊢
    constructor <;> linarith [a1.1, a1.2, a2.1, a2.2]

/-- **No chordless cycles in the prime Rips graph.**  At every scale `ε`, a cycle of
length `≥ 4` in the Vietoris–Rips graph of the prime point cloud must have a chord.
So the prime cloud creates no minimal one-cycle at any scale: the conjectured `H₁`
bars at scale `(log x)²` — and in particular a "twin prime `H₁` bar" — do not exist. -/
theorem prime_no_chordless_cycle {ε : ℝ} {k : ℕ} (hk : 4 ≤ k) {c : ℕ → ℕ}
    (hper : ∀ i, c (i + k) = c i) (hinj : ∀ i < k, ∀ j < k, c i = c j → i = j)
    (hadj : ∀ i, RipsAdj P ε (c i) (c (i + 1)))
    (hchordless : ∀ t, ¬ RipsAdj P ε (c t) (c (t + 2))) : False := by
  obtain ⟨t, -, hchord⟩ :=
    cycle_has_two_step_chord P_strictMono hk hper hinj (fun i => hadj i)
  exact hchordless t hchord

/-- The prime Rips graph does have chords to find: at scale `ε ≥ 4` the three
consecutive primes `3, 5, 7` form a triangle, so the chord statement above is not
vacuous. -/
theorem prime_triangle_at_scale_four : RipsAdj P 4 1 3 := by
  have h1 : P 1 = 3 := by simp [P]
  have h3 : P 3 = 7 := by
    have h7 : Nat.nth Nat.Prime 3 = 7 := by simp
    simp [P, h7]
  unfold RipsAdj
  rw [h1, h3]
  rw [abs_le]
  constructor <;> norm_num

/-- Being in the same `ε`-connected component: the reflexive–transitive closure
of the (symmetric) Rips adjacency relation. -/
def RipsConn (p : ℕ → ℝ) (ε : ℝ) : ℕ → ℕ → Prop :=
  Relation.ReflTransGen (RipsAdj p ε)

  linarith [ hp.monotone h1, hp.monotone ( Nat.succ_le_of_lt h2 ) ]

  · intro k hk₁ hk₂; linarith [ abs_le.mp h, hp.monotone hk₁, hp.monotone ( Nat.le_succ k ), hp.monotone hk₂ ] ;

  induction h <;> simp_all +decide;

consecutive gap between them is at most `ε`.

when `ε` reaches the gap `p_{i+1} - p_i`; i.e. the `i`-th finite `H_0` bar has
death scale equal to that gap.

open Finset

open PrimePH

/-! ## Chains, degrees and cycles over `𝔽₂` -/

/-- An ordered edge `(a, b)`, `a < b`, of the Vietoris–Rips graph at scale `ε`. -/
def IsRipsEdge (p : ℕ → ℝ) (ε : ℝ) (e : ℕ × ℕ) : Prop := e.1 < e.2 ∧ |p e.1 - p e.2| ≤ ε

/-- The edges of a chain incident to a vertex. -/
def inc (E : Finset (ℕ × ℕ)) (v : ℕ) : Finset (ℕ × ℕ) :=
  E.filter (fun e => e.1 = v ∨ e.2 = v)

/-- The degree of a vertex in a `1`-chain. -/
def deg (E : Finset (ℕ × ℕ)) (v : ℕ) : ℕ := (inc E v).card

/-- A `1`-chain is a cycle (`∂₁ = 0` over `𝔽₂`) iff every degree is even. -/
def IsCycleChain (E : Finset (ℕ × ℕ)) : Prop := ∀ v, Even (deg E v)

/-- The boundary of the triangle `a < b < c`, as a `1`-chain. -/
def triangleChain (a b c : ℕ) : Finset (ℕ × ℕ) := {(a, b), (b, c), (a, c)}

/-- The span of the boundaries of the Rips triangles: the image of `∂₂` over `𝔽₂`. -/
inductive TriangleSpan (p : ℕ → ℝ) (ε : ℝ) : Finset (ℕ × ℕ) → Prop
  | zero : TriangleSpan p ε ∅
  | add {a b c : ℕ} {E : Finset (ℕ × ℕ)} (hab : a < b) (hbc : b < c)
      (h1 : IsRipsEdge p ε (a, b)) (h2 : IsRipsEdge p ε (b, c))
      (h3 : IsRipsEdge p ε (a, c)) (hE : TriangleSpan p ε E) :
      TriangleSpan p ε (symmDiff (triangleChain a b c) E)

/-! ## Counting lemmas -/

/-- Cardinalities add modulo `2` under symmetric difference. -/
theorem card_symmDiff_add (A B : Finset (ℕ × ℕ)) :
    (symmDiff A B).card + 2 * (A ∩ B).card = A.card + B.card := by
  have h1 : symmDiff A B = (A ∪ B) \ (A ∩ B) := by
    ext x; simp [Finset.mem_symmDiff]; tauto
  have h4 : A ∩ B ∩ (A ∪ B) = A ∩ B := by ext x; simp
  have h2 : (A ∩ B) ⊆ (A ∪ B) := by intro x hx; simp at hx ⊢; tauto
  have h3 : (A ∩ B).card ≤ (A ∪ B).card := Finset.card_le_card h2
  rw [h1, Finset.card_sdiff, h4]
  have := Finset.card_union_add_card_inter A B
  omega

/-- Weights add modulo the intersection under symmetric difference. -/
theorem sum_symmDiff_add (f : ℕ × ℕ → ℕ) (A B : Finset (ℕ × ℕ)) :
    (∑ e ∈ symmDiff A B, f e) + 2 * (∑ e ∈ A ∩ B, f e)
      = (∑ e ∈ A, f e) + ∑ e ∈ B, f e := by
  have h1 : symmDiff A B = (A ∪ B) \ (A ∩ B) := by
    ext x; simp [Finset.mem_symmDiff]; tauto
  have h2 : (A ∩ B) ⊆ (A ∪ B) := by intro x hx; simp at hx ⊢; tauto
  have h3 := Finset.sum_sdiff (f := f) h2
  have h4 := Finset.sum_union_inter (s₁ := A) (s₂ := B) (f := f)
  rw [h1]
  omega

/-- The weight of a chain: the sum of the right endpoints of its edges. -/
def weight (E : Finset (ℕ × ℕ)) : ℕ := ∑ e ∈ E, e.2

/-- Weights add modulo the intersection under symmetric difference. -/
theorem weight_symmDiff (A B : Finset (ℕ × ℕ)) :
    weight (symmDiff A B) + 2 * (∑ e ∈ A ∩ B, e.2) = weight A + weight B :=
  sum_symmDiff_add (fun e => e.2) A B

/-- Incidence sets commute with symmetric difference. -/
theorem inc_symmDiff (A B : Finset (ℕ × ℕ)) (v : ℕ) :
    inc (symmDiff A B) v = symmDiff (inc A v) (inc B v) := by
  ext x
  simp [inc, Finset.mem_symmDiff]
  tauto

/-- Degrees add modulo `2` under symmetric difference. -/
theorem deg_symmDiff (A B : Finset (ℕ × ℕ)) (v : ℕ) :
    deg (symmDiff A B) v + 2 * (inc A v ∩ inc B v).card = deg A v + deg B v := by
  unfold deg
  rw [inc_symmDiff]
  exact card_symmDiff_add _ _

/-- Every vertex of a triangle has degree `2` in it; all other vertices degree `0`. -/
theorem deg_triangle (a b c v : ℕ) (hab : a < b) (hbc : b < c) :
    deg (triangleChain a b c) v = if v = a ∨ v = b ∨ v = c then 2 else 0 := by
  have n1 : a ≠ b := hab.ne
  have n2 : b ≠ c := hbc.ne
  have n3 : a ≠ c := (hab.trans hbc).ne
  have m1 : b ≠ a := hab.ne'
  have m2 : c ≠ b := hbc.ne'
  have m3 : c ≠ a := (hab.trans hbc).ne'
  unfold deg inc triangleChain
  rw [Finset.filter_insert, Finset.filter_insert, Finset.filter_singleton]
  by_cases h1 : v = a
  · simp_all [Prod.ext_iff, Finset.card_insert_of_notMem]
  by_cases h2 : v = b
  · simp_all [Prod.ext_iff, Finset.card_insert_of_notMem]
  by_cases h3 : v = c
  · simp_all [Prod.ext_iff, Finset.card_insert_of_notMem]
  · have k1 : a ≠ v := fun h => h1 h.symm
    have k2 : b ≠ v := fun h => h2 h.symm
    have k3 : c ≠ v := fun h => h3 h.symm
    simp [k1, k2, k3, h1, h2, h3]

/-- A triangle is itself a cycle. -/
theorem isCycleChain_triangle {a b c : ℕ} (hab : a < b) (hbc : b < c) :
    IsCycleChain (triangleChain a b c) := by
  intro v
  rw [deg_triangle a b c v hab hbc]
  split <;> decide

/-- The weight of a triangle `a < b < c`. -/
theorem weight_triangle {a b c : ℕ} (hab : a < b) (hbc : b < c) :
    weight (triangleChain a b c) = b + c + c := by
  have n1 : ((a, b) : ℕ × ℕ) ≠ (b, c) := by simp [Prod.ext_iff]; omega
  have n2 : ((a, b) : ℕ × ℕ) ≠ (a, c) := by simp [Prod.ext_iff]; omega
  have n3 : ((b, c) : ℕ × ℕ) ≠ (a, c) := by simp [Prod.ext_iff]; omega
  unfold weight triangleChain
  rw [Finset.sum_insert (by simp [n1, n2]), Finset.sum_insert (by simp [n3])]
  simp
  omega

theorem cycle_mem_triangleSpan {p : ℕ → ℝ} (hp : StrictMono p) {ε : ℝ}

import Computation.PrimeBarcodePoissonObstruction

open scoped Classical

namespace PrimeBarcodeCorr

/-! ## The exclusion rule -/

/-- **The mod-3 law of the prime barcode.**  For every `i ≥ 2` at least one of the two
consecutive bar lengths `g_i`, `g_{i+1}`, or their sum, is divisible by `3`.  Reason:
`p`, `p + g_i`, `p + g_i + g_{i+1}` are three primes `> 3`, so their residues mod `3`
lie in `{1, 2}` and two of them must coincide. -/
theorem gap_pair_mod_three {i : ℕ} (hi : 2 ≤ i) :
    3 ∣ primeGap i ∨ 3 ∣ primeGap (i + 1) ∨ 3 ∣ (primeGap i + primeGap (i + 1)) := by
  have hlt1 := Nat.nth_strictMono (p := Nat.Prime) Nat.infinite_setOf_prime (Nat.lt_succ_self i)
  have hlt2 :=
    Nat.nth_strictMono (p := Nat.Prime) Nat.infinite_setOf_prime (Nat.lt_succ_self (i + 1))

  rw [show i.succ = i + 1 from rfl] at hlt1

    have h := Nat.nth_monotone (p := Nat.Prime) Nat.infinite_setOf_prime hi
    simpa using h

  have hp1 : Nat.Prime (Nat.nth Nat.Prime (i + 1)) := Nat.prime_nth_prime (i + 1)
  have hp2 : Nat.Prime (Nat.nth Nat.Prime (i + 2)) := Nat.prime_nth_prime (i + 2)

    intro hd; rcases hp0.eq_one_or_self_of_dvd 3 hd with h | h <;> omega
  have n1 : ¬ (3 ∣ Nat.nth Nat.Prime (i + 1)) := by
    intro hd; rcases hp1.eq_one_or_self_of_dvd 3 hd with h | h <;> omega
  have n2 : ¬ (3 ∣ Nat.nth Nat.Prime (i + 2)) := by
    intro hd; rcases hp2.eq_one_or_self_of_dvd 3 hd with h | h <;> omega

  have e2 : primeGap (i + 1) = Nat.nth Nat.Prime (i + 2) - Nat.nth Nat.Prime (i + 1) := by
    show Nat.nth Nat.Prime (i + 1 + 1) - _ = _
    norm_num
  omega

adjacent bars of equal length `g` force `3 ∣ g`. -/
theorem repeated_gap_dvd_three {i : ℕ} (hi : 2 ≤ i) (h : primeGap i = primeGap (i + 1)) :

  rcases gap_pair_mod_three hi with hd | hd | hd

theorem no_two_consecutive_twin_bars {i : ℕ} (hi : 2 ≤ i) :
    ¬ (primeGap i = 2 ∧ primeGap (i + 1) = 2) := by
  rintro ⟨h1, h2⟩

  rw [h1] at this
  omega

theorem no_two_consecutive_cousin_bars {i : ℕ} (hi : 2 ≤ i) :
    ¬ (primeGap i = 4 ∧ primeGap (i + 1) = 4) := by
  rintro ⟨h1, h2⟩

/-- The number of adjacent twin-bar pairs among the first `n` bars, past the start. -/

  ((Finset.range n).filter
    (fun i => 2 ≤ i ∧ primeGap i = 2 ∧ primeGap (i + 1) = 2)).card

  nlinarith

from __future__ import annotations

import math
from collections import Counter
from typing import Dict, Iterable, List, Sequence, Set, Tuple

Edge = Tuple[int, int]


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. The point cloud
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------

def primes_upto(limit: int) -> List[int]:
    """All primes <= limit by a simple sieve of Eratosthenes."""
    sieve = bytearray([1]) * (limit + 1)
    sieve[0:2] = b"\x00\x00"
    for i in range(2, int(limit ** 0.5) + 1):
        if sieve[i]:
            sieve[i * i::i] = bytearray(len(sieve[i * i::i]))
    return [i for i in range(limit + 1) if sieve[i]]


def gaps_of(primes: Sequence[int]) -> List[int]:
    """The H_0 bar lengths: g_i = p_{i+1} - p_i."""
    return [primes[i + 1] - primes[i] for i in range(len(primes) - 1)]


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Barcode invariants
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------

def betti_zero(gaps: Sequence[int], eps: float, n: int) -> int:
    """b_0(eps, n) = 1 + #{ i < n : g_i > eps }, the number of eps-components."""
    return 1 + sum(1 for i in range(min(n, len(gaps))) if gaps[i] > eps)


def betti_area(gaps: Sequence[int], n: int) -> int:
    """Area under the reduced Betti curve = sum of the first n bar lengths."""
    return sum(gaps[:n])


def bar_count_in_window(gaps: Sequence[int], a: float, b: float) -> int:
    """Number of bars whose length lies in the open interval (a, b)."""
    return sum(1 for g in gaps if a < g < b)


def exponential_window_mass(a: float, b: float, mean: float) -> float:
    """Mass of the open window (a,b) under an exponential law with the given mean."""
    return math.exp(-a / mean) - math.exp(-b / mean)


def gap_histogram_from_betti(gaps: Sequence[int], k: int, n: int) -> int:
    """Inversion formula: #{ i<n : g_i = 2k } = b_0(2k-1, n) - b_0(2k+1, n)."""
    return betti_zero(gaps, 2 * k - 1, n) - betti_zero(gaps, 2 * k + 1, n)


def twin_step(gaps: Sequence[int], n: int) -> int:
    """The eps = 2 step of the Betti staircase, b_0(1,n) - b_0(2,n)."""
    return betti_zero(gaps, 1, n) - betti_zero(gaps, 2, n)


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. F_2 one-chains of a Rips complex on a line, and the vanishing of H_1

def is_rips_edge(cloud: Sequence[float], eps: float, e: Edge) -> bool:
    """(a,b) with a < b is an edge iff |x_a - x_b| <= eps."""
    a, b = e
    return a < b and abs(cloud[a] - cloud[b]) <= eps


def degrees(chain: Iterable[Edge]) -> Dict[int, int]:
    """Vertex degrees of an F_2 one-chain (a finite set of edges)."""
    deg: Counter = Counter()
    for a, b in chain:
        deg[a] += 1
        deg[b] += 1
    return dict(deg)


def is_cycle(chain: Set[Edge]) -> bool:
    """A one-chain is a cycle (boundary zero over F_2) iff all degrees are even."""
    return all(d % 2 == 0 for d in degrees(chain).values())


def weight(chain: Iterable[Edge]) -> int:
    """The termination measure mu(E) = sum of the right endpoints of the edges."""
    return sum(b for _a, b in chain)


def symm_diff(a: Set[Edge], b: Set[Edge]) -> Set[Edge]:
    return a ^ b


def triangle_chain(a: int, b: int, c: int) -> Set[Edge]:
    """The boundary of the triangle a < b < c."""
    return {(a, b), (b, c), (a, c)}


def decompose_cycle_into_triangles(
    cloud: Sequence[float], eps: float, chain: Set[Edge]
) -> List[Tuple[int, int, int]]:
    """
    Write an F_2 one-cycle of a line Rips complex as a sum of Rips triangles.

    Repeatedly take the largest vertex v carried by the chain.  Its degree is even and
    positive, so two edges (u,v) and (w,v) with u < w < v are present.  Because x_u and
    x_w both lie in the window [x_v - eps, x_v], the chord (u,w) is itself a Rips edge,
    so T = {(u,w),(w,v),(u,v)} is a Rips triangle; replacing the chain by T + chain
    keeps it a cycle and strictly decreases the weight mu.  Terminates in at most mu
    steps and returns the list of triangles used.
    """
    triangles: List[Tuple[int, int, int]] = []
    work = set(chain)
    while work:
        assert is_cycle(work), "invariant: the working chain stays a cycle"
        v = max(max(e) for e in work)
        incident = sorted(a for (a, b) in work if b == v)
        if len(incident) < 2:
            raise ValueError("degree at the maximal vertex must be even and positive")
        u, w = incident[0], incident[1]
        assert is_rips_edge(cloud, eps, (u, w)), "the chord must be a Rips edge"
        tri = triangle_chain(u, w, v)
        before = weight(work)
        work = symm_diff(tri, work)
        assert weight(work) < before, "the weight must strictly decrease"
        triangles.append((u, w, v))
    return triangles

# 4. Arithmetic correlation laws of the barcode

def adjacent_pair_histogram(gaps: Sequence[int]) -> Counter:
    """Histogram of adjacent bar-length pairs (g_i, g_{i+1})."""
    return Counter((gaps[i], gaps[i + 1]) for i in range(len(gaps) - 1))


def smallest_block_divisible(gaps: Sequence[int], primes: Sequence[int],
                             q: int, i: int) -> Tuple[int, int, int]:
    """
    Find j < k < q with q | g_i + ... + g_{i+k-1} - (g_i + ... + g_{i+j-1}).

    Guaranteed to exist whenever p_i > q, by the pigeonhole principle applied to the
    residues mod q of the q primes p_i, ..., p_{i+q-1}, none of which is 0 mod q.
    """
    partial = [0]
    for m in range(q):
        partial.append(partial[-1] + gaps[i + m])
    seen: Dict[int, int] = {}
    base = primes[i] % q
    for j in range(q):
        r = (base + partial[j]) % q
        if r in seen:
            return seen[r], j, partial[j] - partial[seen[r]]
        seen[r] = j
    raise AssertionError("pigeonhole guarantees a repeat")

from collections import Counter
from typing import Dict, List, Sequence, Tuple

def primes_upto(limit: int) -> List[int]:
    """Primes <= limit, by the sieve of Eratosthenes."""
    sieve = bytearray([1]) * (limit + 1)
    sieve[0:2] = b"\x00\x00"
    for i in range(2, int(limit ** 0.5) + 1):
        if sieve[i]:

    """The H_0 bar lengths of the prime point cloud."""
    return [primes[i + 1] - primes[i] for i in range(len(primes) - 1)]


def twin_step(gaps: Sequence[int], n: int) -> int:
    """tau(n) = b_0(1,n) - b_0(2,n) = number of bars of length exactly 2 among the first n."""
    return sum(1 for g in gaps[:n] if g == 2)

    """The conjectural twin-pair count below x: 2 * Pi_2 * x / (log x)^2."""
    return 2.0 * TWIN_PRIME_CONSTANT * x / (math.log(x) ** 2)

    """Counts of adjacent equal bar pairs (d, d)."""
    return Counter(gaps[i] for i in range(len(gaps) - 1) if gaps[i] == gaps[i + 1])

                     i: int) -> Tuple[int, int, int]:

    seen: Dict[int, int] = {}
    base = primes[i] % q
    for j in range(q):

        if r in seen:

        seen[r] = j
    raise AssertionError("pigeonhole on q-1 residue classes guarantees a repeat")

    "algorithm_barcode_extraction": """"Algorithm A: extraction of the zero-dimensional prime barcode."""

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import Dict, List, Sequence, Tuple


def sieve_primes(limit: int) -> List[int]:
    """All primes <= limit in O(limit log log limit) time and O(limit) bits of space."""
    sieve = bytearray([1]) * (limit + 1)
    sieve[0:2] = b"\x00\x00"
    step = 2
    while step * step <= limit:
        if sieve[step]:
            sieve[step * step::step] = bytearray(len(sieve[step * step::step]))
        step += 1
    return [i for i in range(limit + 1) if sieve[i]]


def prime_barcode(limit: int) -> Tuple[List[int], List[Tuple[float, float]]]:
    """
    Return (primes, bars) where bars are the finite H_0 intervals of the Rips filtration.

    On a line two points merge exactly when the scale reaches the gap separating their
    components, so the i-th finite bar is [0, p_{i+1} - p_i).  There is in addition a
    single infinite bar, omitted here.
    """
    primes = sieve_primes(limit)
    bars = [(0.0, float(primes[i + 1] - primes[i])) for i in range(len(primes) - 1)]
    return primes, bars


def bar_length_histogram(bars: Sequence[Tuple[float, float]]) -> Dict[int, int]:
    """Multiplicity of each bar length; supported on {1} union the even integers."""
    hist: Dict[int, int] = {}
    for birth, death in bars:
        length = int(round(death - birth))
        hist[length] = hist.get(length, 0) + 1
    return hist


def total_persistence(bars: Sequence[Tuple[float, float]]) -> float:
    """Sum of the bar lengths; equals p_n - 2 and equals the reduced Betti area."""
    return sum(death - birth for birth, death in bars)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    primes, bars = prime_barcode(10 ** 5)
    hist = bar_length_histogram(bars)
    print(f"{len(bars)} finite bars; length spectrum {sorted(hist)[:12]} ...")
    print(f"odd lengths present: {[d for d in hist if d % 2 == 1]}")
    print(f"total persistence {total_persistence(bars):.0f} = p_n - 2 = {primes[-1] - 2}")

    "algorithm_betti_staircase": """"Algorithm B: the Betti staircase, its area, and inversion to the gap histogram."""

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import Dict, List, Sequence, Tuple


def betti_staircase(gaps: Sequence[int]) -> List[Tuple[int, int]]:
    """
    The complete Betti staircase of the prime cloud as a list of (threshold, value) pairs.

    b_0(eps, n) = 1 + #{ i < n : g_i > eps } is a right-continuous decreasing step
    function whose jumps occur only at even integers (and at 1).  One suffix-sum over the
    gap histogram produces every value at once, in O(g_max) time after an O(n) histogram
    pass.
    """
    hist: Dict[int, int] = {}
    for g in gaps:
        hist[g] = hist.get(g, 0) + 1
    g_max = max(hist)
    tail = 0
    staircase: List[Tuple[int, int]] = []
    for eps in range(g_max, -1, -1):
        staircase.append((eps, 1 + tail))
        tail += hist.get(eps, 0)
    staircase.reverse()
    return staircase


def betti_value(staircase: Sequence[Tuple[int, int]], eps: float) -> int:
    """Evaluate the staircase at an arbitrary real scale (it is constant on [2k, 2k+2))."""
    value = staircase[0][1]
    for threshold, v in staircase:
        if threshold <= eps:
            value = v
        else:
            break
    return value


def betti_area(gaps: Sequence[int]) -> int:
    """Area under the reduced Betti curve = sum of bar lengths = p_n - 2."""
    return sum(gaps)


def gap_histogram_from_staircase(staircase: Sequence[Tuple[int, int]],
                                 k_max: int) -> Dict[int, int]:
    """
    Inversion: #{ i : g_i = 2k } = b_0(2k-1) - b_0(2k+1).

    The Betti staircase and the gap histogram are therefore equivalent data, related by
    prefix/suffix differencing in linear time.
    """
    return {2 * k: betti_value(staircase, 2 * k - 1) - betti_value(staircase, 2 * k + 1)
            for k in range(1, k_max + 1)}


if __name__ == "__main__":

    primes = sieve_primes(10 ** 5)
    gaps = [primes[i + 1] - primes[i] for i in range(len(primes) - 1)]
    stair = betti_staircase(gaps)
    print("b_0 is constant on [2k, 2k+2):",
          {betti_value(stair, 4 + t) for t in (0.0, 0.5, 1.0, 1.99)})
    print("area under reduced Betti curve:", betti_area(gaps), "= p_n - 2 =", primes[-1] - 2)
    inverted = gap_histogram_from_staircase(stair, 6)
    print("inverted histogram:", inverted)

    "algorithm_cycle_reduction": """"Algorithm C: constructive vanishing of H_1 for a point cloud on a line."""

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import Dict, Iterable, List, Sequence, Set, Tuple

Edge = Tuple[int, int]
Triangle = Tuple[int, int, int]


def is_rips_edge(cloud: Sequence[float], eps: float, edge: Edge) -> bool:
    """(a,b) with a < b is an edge of the scale-eps complex iff |x_a - x_b| <= eps."""
    a, b = edge
    return a < b and abs(cloud[a] - cloud[b]) <= eps


def degrees(chain: Iterable[Edge]) -> Dict[int, int]:
    """Vertex degrees of an F_2 one-chain."""
    deg: Dict[int, int] = {}
    for a, b in chain:
        deg[a] = deg.get(a, 0) + 1
        deg[b] = deg.get(b, 0) + 1
    return deg


def is_cycle(chain: Set[Edge]) -> bool:
    """Over F_2 the boundary of a chain is its set of odd-degree vertices."""
    return all(d % 2 == 0 for d in degrees(chain).values())


def weight(chain: Iterable[Edge]) -> int:
    """The termination measure mu(E) = sum of the right endpoints of the edges of E."""
    return sum(b for _a, b in chain)


def reduce_cycle_to_triangles(cloud: Sequence[float], eps: float,
                              cycle: Set[Edge]) -> List[Triangle]:
    """
    Write an F_2 one-cycle of a line Rips complex as a sum of Rips triangles.

    Invariant: the working chain is always a cycle of Rips edges.  Each iteration takes
    the maximal vertex v carried by the chain; its degree is even and nonzero, so two
    edges (u,v) and (w,v) with u < w < v are present.  Since x_u and x_w both lie in the
    window [x_v - eps, x_v], the chord (u,w) is a Rips edge, so T = {(u,w),(w,v),(u,v)}
    is a Rips triangle.  Adding T keeps all degrees even and strictly lowers mu, because
    two edges of weight v disappear and at most one of weight w < v appears.  Hence the
    loop performs at most mu(cycle) iterations and returns a decomposition certifying
    that the cycle bounds -- a constructive proof that H_1 vanishes at every scale.
    """
    triangles: List[Triangle] = []
    work: Set[Edge] = set(cycle)
    if not all(is_rips_edge(cloud, eps, e) for e in work):
        raise ValueError("input chain must consist of Rips edges at this scale")
    if not is_cycle(work):
        raise ValueError("input chain must be a cycle (all degrees even)")
    while work:
        v = max(b for _a, b in work)
        left = sorted(a for (a, b) in work if b == v)
        u, w = left[0], left[1]
        triangle: Set[Edge] = {(u, w), (w, v), (u, v)}
        before = weight(work)
        work ^= triangle
        assert weight(work) < before
        triangles.append((u, w, v))
    return triangles


if __name__ == "__main__":
    cloud = [2.0, 3.0, 5.0, 7.0, 11.0, 13.0, 17.0]
    quad: Set[Edge] = {(1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 4), (1, 4)}     # the primes 3, 5, 7, 11
    print("cycle:", sorted(quad), "degrees:", degrees(quad))
    tris = reduce_cycle_to_triangles(cloud, 8.0, quad)
    print("decomposition:", [tuple(int(cloud[i]) for i in t) for t in tris])

primes below 10^6.  Every empty cell is an instance of the mod-3 law: for three
consecutive primes past 3, one of a, b, a+b must be divisible by 3, so a pair (a,b) with
none of a, b, a+b divisible by 3 can never occur.  The diagonal is therefore empty except
at multiples of 3 ("two adjacent bars of equal length d force 3 | d"), while a model with
independent bar lengths would give every cell positive frequency.

Right panel: the geometry behind the vanishing of H_1.  A one-cycle of the scale-eps
complex of a point cloud on a line always has, at its rightmost vertex v, two incident
edges (u,v) and (w,v) with u < w < v; since x_u and x_w both lie in the window
[x_v - eps, x_v], the chord (u,w) is present and the triangle (u,w,v) can be cancelled,
strictly reducing the weight of the cycle.  The panel draws one step of this reduction on
the prime quadrilateral 3, 5, 7, 11 at scale eps = 8.

Requires matplotlib and numpy.  Saves prime_barcode_correlations.png.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import List

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np


def primes_upto(limit: int) -> List[int]:
    sieve = bytearray([1]) * (limit + 1)
    sieve[0:2] = b"\x00\x00"
    for i in range(2, int(limit ** 0.5) + 1):
        if sieve[i]:
            sieve[i * i::i] = bytearray(len(sieve[i * i::i]))
    return [i for i in range(limit + 1) if sieve[i]]


def main() -> None:
    primes = primes_upto(10 ** 6)
    gaps = [primes[i + 1] - primes[i] for i in range(len(primes) - 1)]

    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(15, 6.5))

    # ---- adjacent-pair heat map -------------------------------------------------
    m = 12                       # bar lengths 2, 4, ..., 24
    matrix = np.zeros((m, m))
    for i in range(len(gaps) - 1):
        a, b = gaps[i], gaps[i + 1]
        if a % 2 == 0 and b % 2 == 0 and a <= 2 * m and b <= 2 * m:
            matrix[a // 2 - 1, b // 2 - 1] += 1
    ax = axes[0]
    im = ax.imshow(np.log10(matrix + 1), origin="lower", cmap="magma",
                   extent=(1, 2 * m + 1, 1, 2 * m + 1))
    ax.set_xticks(range(2, 2 * m + 1, 2))
    ax.set_yticks(range(2, 2 * m + 1, 2))
    ax.set_xlabel("length of bar $i+1$")
    ax.set_ylabel("length of bar $i$")
    ax.set_title("Adjacent bar pairs $(g_i, g_{i+1})$, log counts.  Black cells are the\n"
                 "mod-3 exclusions: $3 \\nmid a$, $3 \\nmid b$, $3 \\nmid (a+b)$ is impossible")
    for a in range(2, 2 * m + 1, 2):
        for b in range(2, 2 * m + 1, 2):
            if a % 3 and b % 3 and (a + b) % 3:
                ax.plot(b, a, marker="x", color="#5ee0ff", ms=7, mew=1.6)
    fig.colorbar(im, ax=ax, label=r"$\log_{10}(1+\mathrm{count})$")

    # ---- the reduction step -----------------------------------------------------
    ax = axes[1]
    pts = [3, 5, 7, 11]
    ys = [0.0] * 4
    ax.scatter(pts, ys, s=90, color="#22456b", zorder=3)
    for x in pts:
        ax.annotate(str(x), (x, 0.0), textcoords="offset points", xytext=(0, -22),
                    ha="center", fontsize=12)

    def arc(x0: float, x1: float, height: float, colour: str, style: str, label: str = "") -> None:
        t = np.linspace(0, np.pi, 200)
        cx, r = (x0 + x1) / 2, (x1 - x0) / 2
        ax.plot(cx + r * np.cos(t), height * np.sin(t), color=colour, ls=style, lw=2.2,
                label=label)

    arc(3, 5, 0.35, "#22456b", "-", "cycle edges")
    arc(5, 7, 0.35, "#22456b", "-")
    arc(7, 11, 0.5, "#22456b", "-")
    arc(3, 11, 0.95, "#22456b", "-")
    arc(3, 7, 0.62, "#c1440e", "--", r"chord (present since $\varepsilon=8$)")
    ax.axhline(0, color="k", lw=1)
    ax.set_ylim(-0.35, 1.25)
    ax.set_xlim(1.5, 12.5)
    ax.set_yticks([])
    ax.set_title(r"Killing a cycle at scale $\varepsilon=8$:"
                 "\n"
                 r"$\{3\!-\!5,5\!-\!7,7\!-\!11,3\!-\!11\}=T(3,5,7)+T(3,7,11)$")
    ax.set_xlabel("position on the line")
    ax.legend(loc="upper right")

    fig.tight_layout()
    fig.savefig("prime_barcode_correlations.png", dpi=160)
    print("wrote prime_barcode_correlations.png")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
"
  },
  "lean_files": [
    "Catalog/Computation/PrimeBarcodePoissonObstruction.lean",
    "Catalog/Computation/LineRipsH1Vanishing.lean",
    "Catalog/Computation/PrimeBarcodeCorrelations.lean",
    "Catalog/Computation/PrimeBettiCurveIntegral.lean"
  ]
}

concept.title: Compression Research B5: PRNG-generated real-world data — detection and seed recovery
concept.concept_description:
**Part of:** Research plan — *Compression Beyond the Pigeonhole Bound* (Phase B, Question 2: can random number generators help?).

## Research question
A surprising amount of real-world data **is** PRNG output: game worlds, simulations, certain file formats, crypto keys. Detect it and recover the seed → compress to ~0 bits beyond the seed.

## Approach
- Robust **PRNG fingerprinting**: which generator family produced this stream?
- **Seed recovery**: Berlekamp–Massey for LFSRs; solver-based inversion for other families.
- A classifier that routes each file to *seed-compressible* vs. *model-compressible*.

## Deliverable
Detection + seed-recovery tooling and a benchmark of seed-compressible files found in real corpora.

## Falsifiability / gate
For a recovered seed: decompressed output must exactly reproduce the file. Measures what fraction of real data is seed-compressible.

**Milestone:** M2 (cheap, warm-up infrastructure). Related: [[B1]].

            ## v19 Research Core Methodology — Speculative Scientific-Method Loop

You are the Principal Investigator leading a speculative research team with four
roles: **Hypothesizer**, **Experimenter**, **Analyst**, and **Critic**. This engine
is configured for **Speculative Specifying (Bold Conjectures)**: target high-risk,
high-reward, grand-challenge level research while maintaining adversarial rigor.

### Stage 1 — Hypothesize (team: Hypothesizer)
Brainstorm 5–7 falsifiable conjectures about the topic. At least three must be
bold, surprising, or grand-challenge level. Rank them by expected scientific
impact, not by ease of proof.
**CRITICAL SCORING REQUIREMENT**: To maximize your Phase A quality score, your
conjectures MUST aim for extreme `proof_depth` (deep structural hierarchies rather
than shallow one-liners) and `cross_domain` bridging (combining distinct areas of
math, e.g., algebra with topology, or geometry with combinatorics).

### Stage 2 — Experiment (team: Experimenter)
For each conjecture, attempt to prove it in Lean 4 or disprove it with a concrete
counterexample. Prioritize the boldest conjectures first. If a proof is beyond
reach, prove the strongest lemma you can and mark the remaining step with exactly
one `sorry` that is clearly documented.

### Stage 3 — Analyze (team: Analyst)
Summarize what survived, what failed, and **why** failures failed. Distinguish
"true but hard", "false", and "needs a different definition". Extract structural
patterns that could unify several observations.

### Stage 4 — Critique / Adversarial Review (team: Critic)
Before finalizing, challenge every theorem:
- Is any theorem trivial (True, definitional equality, `native_decide`)?
- Does every main theorem have 0 sorries?
- Do the results genuinely extend the attached catalog files?
- Are there hidden assumptions or corner cases that break the claim?
If you find a weakness, fix it or replace the theorem with a guarded version and
explain the boundary.

### Stage 5 — Synthesize (team: Principal Investigator)
Combine the verified results into clean, compiling Lean 4 files.
Write a `FUTURE_DIRECTIONS.md` that lists 3–5 **bold, testable** conjectures
derived from Stage 3 and Stage 4. Each conjecture must include a
"The key insight is..." sentence and a "Why now?" justification.

### Perpetual Scientific Iteration (do not stop at first synthesis)
When the research team comes together with results, do not stop. Treat the
synthesized findings as the next problem statement and immediately run the full
scientific-method loop again: hypothesize, experiment, review, synthesize,
critique. Repeat this cycle continuously within the available context window,
refining, deepening, and cross-checking until forced to emit output. Use
Aristotle to its fullest.

### Anti-Trivial Guardrails
- Do not produce trivial proofs (`True := by trivial`, `rfl`-only, `Inhabited X`-only, `native_decide`-only).
- Use an insight-bearing tactic (e.g. `induction`, `nlinarith`, `omega`, `field_simp`).

### Self-Critique Checklist
- No theorem is trivial.
- Every main theorem has 0 sorries.
- Lab Notes blocks contain real experimental data.

### Strictly Forbidden in Phase A
Do NOT create packaging deliverables in Phase A: `ARTICLE.md`, `RESEARCH_PAPER.md`, `demo.py`, `PACKAGE.json`.

### Recursive Abduction / Thread Continuation (v19c)
If prior-cycle context is provided, treat it as a live research thread: refine
the hypotheses from the previous cycle, attempt to close open conjectures, and
produce three concrete next-cycle sub-conjectures. If no prior context is
provided, still run a self-contained abductive loop: generate conjectures, test
them, and immediately spin off the most promising follow-up conjectures as
future directions.


            ## Hard Constraints
            1. Every theorem MUST be fully proved (0 sorries, no stubbed signatures).
            2. No circular proofs (a theorem must never reference itself directly or transitively in its proof).
            3. No trivial results (e.g. `True := by trivial`, `rfl`-only, `native_decide`-only).
            4. All files must be self-contained and compilable with Lean 4 (mathlib4 v4.28.0).
            5. Build directly on existing catalog definitions — do not re-invent.

            ## Output Requirements
            Return ONLY:
            1. `.lean` files in `Catalog/MachineLearning/` with complete formal proofs.
            2. `FUTURE_DIRECTIONS.md` with 3–5 concrete, falsifiable conjectures derived from your findings.
            3. `SELF_EVALUATION.json` with your honest self-assessment of the research:
               {
                 "quality_score": <float 0.0 to 1.0>,
                 "proof_depth": <float 0.0 to 1.0>,
                 "novelty": <float 0.0 to 1.0>,
                 "grade": "world_class" | "substantial" | "partial" | "shallow" | "trivial",
                 "rationale": "<2-3 sentence justification of grade and mathematical significance>"
               }

            Focus all compute budget on proving theorems.


### Computational Evidence Stage (Recommended)

Before writing the formal Lean 4 proof, you are strongly encouraged to produce
computational evidence for the claim. Create a file named `ComputationalEvidence.md`
in the project directory with:

1. **Small-case calculations** — compute the first several instances of the object/conjecture.
2. **OEIS search results** — if a sequence appears, note its OEIS ID and first terms.
3. **Counterexample hunt** — test the universal claim on a representative sample; report any counterexample found.
4. **Plots or tables** — include any relevant visual/numerical data.

If you choose to skip this stage, you MUST explicitly justify why computational
evidence is unnecessary or infeasible in a `SkipEvidenceJustification.md` file.

Do not let the evidence stage dominate the project; keep it concise and directly
relevant to the theorem you intend to prove.

concept.title: OR-COLLAPSE-LAW: semiprime OR of a cyclic split-complete fork = g(n) = H((2n-1)/n^2) - (1/n)H(1/n) - ((n-1)/n)H(2/n) bits (round-19 #2, exp 407, v183, paper 72)
concept.concept_description:
## OR-COLLAPSE-LAW (round-19 #2, experiment 407, assessment v183, paper 72)

**An exact universal law of the semiprime OR collapse.** Paper 71 proved the fork-pinning criterion (a fork is congruence-pinned iff it factors through G^ab) and measured one collapse (cond-7 cubic OR = 0.0728 bits). Here is the general law: for any abelian field whose split-completely event is pinned by an order-n Dirichlet character (split ⟺ χ(p)=1, P(split)=1/n), the semiprime OR [split(p) OR split(q)] obeys, for gcd(N,f)=1,

**P(OR | χ(N)=1) = 1/n, P(OR | χ(N)≠1) = 2/n, P(OR) = (2n−1)/n², I(N mod f; OR) = g(n) = H((2n−1)/n²) − (1/n)H(1/n) − ((n−1)/n)H(2/n)** — universal in the order n, independent of field, degree, and conductor structure.

### Machine-verified on 7 fields (2^22, 30k semiprimes, split sets empirically confirmed by nroots==deg)

| field | n | f | I(N mod f; OR) | g(n) |

            ## v19 Research Core Methodology — Speculative Scientific-Method Loop

You are the Principal Investigator leading a speculative research team with four
roles: **Hypothesizer**, **Experimenter**, **Analyst**, and **Critic**. This engine
is configured for **Speculative Specifying (Bold Conjectures)**: target high-risk,
high-reward, grand-challenge level research while maintaining adversarial rigor.

### Stage 1 — Hypothesize (team: Hypothesizer)
Brainstorm 5–7 falsifiable conjectures about the topic. At least three must be
bold, surprising, or grand-challenge level. Rank them by expected scientific
impact, not by ease of proof.
**CRITICAL SCORING REQUIREMENT**: To maximize your Phase A quality score, your
conjectures MUST aim for extreme `proof_depth` (deep structural hierarchies rather
than shallow one-liners) and `cross_domain` bridging (combining distinct areas of
math, e.g., algebra with topology, or geometry with combinatorics).

### Stage 2 — Experiment (team: Experimenter)
For each conjecture, attempt to prove it in Lean 4 or disprove it with a concrete
counterexample. Prioritize the boldest conjectures first. If a proof is beyond
reach, prove the strongest lemma you can and mark the remaining step with exactly
one `sorry` that is clearly documented.

### Stage 3 — Analyze (team: Analyst)
Summarize what survived, what failed, and **why** failures failed. Distinguish
"true but hard", "false", and "needs a different definition". Extract structural
patterns that could unify several observations.

### Stage 4 — Critique / Adversarial Review (team: Critic)
Before finalizing, challenge every theorem:
- Is any theorem trivial (True, definitional equality, `native_decide`)?
- Does every main theorem have 0 sorries?
- Do the results genuinely extend the attached catalog files?
- Are there hidden assumptions or corner cases that break the claim?
If you find a weakness, fix it or replace the theorem with a guarded version and
explain the boundary.

### Stage 5 — Synthesize (team: Principal Investigator)
Combine the verified results into clean, compiling Lean 4 files.
Write a `FUTURE_DIRECTIONS.md` that lists 3–5 **bold, testable** conjectures
derived from Stage 3 and Stage 4. Each conjecture must include a
"The key insight is..." sentence and a "Why now?" justification.

### Perpetual Scientific Iteration (do not stop at first synthesis)
When the research team comes together with results, do not stop. Treat the
synthesized findings as the next problem statement and immediately run the full
scientific-method loop again: hypothesize, experiment, review, synthesize,
critique. Repeat this cycle continuously within the available context window,
refining, deepening, and cross-checking until forced to emit output. Use
Aristotle to its fullest.

### Anti-Trivial Guardrails
- Do not produce trivial proofs (`True := by trivial`, `rfl`-only, `Inhabited X`-only, `native_decide`-only).
- Use an insight-bearing tactic (e.g. `induction`, `nlinarith`, `omega`, `field_simp`).

### Self-Critique Checklist
- No theorem is trivial.
- Every main theorem has 0 sorries.
- Lab Notes blocks contain real experimental data.

### Strictly Forbidden in Phase A
Do NOT create packaging deliverables in Phase A: `ARTICLE.md`, `RESEARCH_PAPER.md`, `demo.py`, `PACKAGE.json`.

### Recursive Abduction / Thread Continuation (v19c)
If prior-cycle context is provided, treat it as a live research thread: refine
the hypotheses from the previous cycle, attempt to close open conjectures, and
produce three concrete next-cycle sub-conjectures. If no prior context is
provided, still run a self-contained abductive loop: generate conjectures, test
them, and immediately spin off the most promising follow-up conjectures as
future directions.


            ## Hard Constraints
            1. Every theorem MUST be fully proved (0 sorries, no stubbed signatures).
            2. No circular proofs (a theorem must never reference itself directly or transitively in its proof).
            3. No trivial results (e.g. `True := by trivial`, `rfl`-only, `native_decide`-only).
            4. All files must be self-contained and compilable with Lean 4 (mathlib4 v4.28.0).
            5. Build directly on existing catalog definitions — do not re-invent.

            ## Output Requirements
            Return ONLY:
            1. `.lean` files in `Catalog/Applications/` with complete formal proofs.
            2. `FUTURE_DIRECTIONS.md` with 3–5 concrete, falsifiable conjectures derived from your findings.
            3. `SELF_EVALUATION.json` with your honest self-assessment of the research:
               {
                 "quality_score": <float 0.0 to 1.0>,
                 "proof_depth": <float 0.0 to 1.0>,
                 "novelty": <float 0.0 to 1.0>,
                 "grade": "world_class" | "substantial" | "partial" | "shallow" | "trivial",
                 "rationale": "<2-3 sentence justification of grade and mathematical significance>"
               }

            Focus all compute budget on proving theorems.


### Computational Evidence Stage (Recommended)

Before writing the formal Lean 4 proof, you are strongly encouraged to produce
computational evidence for the claim. Create a file named `ComputationalEvidence.md`
in the project directory with:

1. **Small-case calculations** — compute the first several instances of the object/conjecture.
2. **OEIS search results** — if a sequence appears, note its OEIS ID and first terms.
3. **Counterexample hunt** — test the universal claim on a representative sample; report any counterexample found.
4. **Plots or tables** — include any relevant visual/numerical data.

If you choose to skip this stage, you MUST explicitly justify why computational
evidence is unnecessary or infeasible in a `SkipEvidenceJustification.md` file.

Do not let the evidence stage dominate the project; keep it concise and directly
relevant to the theorem you intend to prove.

## NET-48 — speed axis (round-net-48; paper 92, /tmp/exp_net_attncost_ctx2048_s3.py, /tmp/net48.log)

**Verdict name: THE-DIRECT-TEST-SURVIVES-VIA-THE-MEDIAN.**

### Result
At (d=4, ctx=2048, seed=3), **k\* = 160 — all four point-horns REFUTED (P1 224, P2 240, P3 256, P4 192: every pre-stated value passes, none is the knee)**, yet the completed 16× three-seed knee distribution **{160, 224, 256} has median EXACTLY 224 = 7/8·(d·ctx/32)**, replicating the 8× median 112 = 7/8·128: **the 7/8-median law is 2/2-context, 6/6-seed.** The horns were point-predictions; the law's claim was the distribution's center — 0/4 horns, 1/1 law. A whole family of third-seed values {160, 192, 224} each keep the median at 224; only ≥256 would shift it.

### The 7/8-median law now two contexts, six seeds
| context | three-seed k\* set | × product | spread | median |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 8× (ctx=1024) | {96, 112, 128} | {0.75, 0.875, 1.0} | 0.25 | 112 = 7/8·128 |
| 16× (ctx=2048) | {160, 224, 256} | {0.625, 0.875, 1.0} | 0.375 | 224 = 7/8·256 |

**The 16× spread is ~50% WIDER than the 8× spread** — the LOW TAIL is the context-growing quantity (0.75 → 0.625), the product value the pinned upper edge (the s1 chain's exactness), the median stable at 7/8. Per-seed knees are too noisy to predict on the point; the distribution's center is the robust quantity — that is what a third seed buys.

### Key numbers
- Full acc 0.1546, bar 0.1516, full loss 5.2199, train **14566s (~4h03m)**.
- Sweep: 96 0.963 ✗, 128 0.973 ✗, **160 0.981 ✓ (margin +0.0012 — the tightest of the recent cells; true knee ~150–160 between grid points)**, 192 0.984 ✓, 224 0.986 ✓, 240 0.987 ✓, **256 0.990 ✓ (product point — passes 3/3)**, 288 0.993 ✓, 384 0.999 ✓, 512 1.000 ✓, 768 1.003 ✓, 1024 1.003 ✓ (loss 5.2215, Δ0.0016). The s3 retained curve is the HIGHEST of the three 16× seeds throughout (0.973 at 128 vs s1 0.939, s2 0.965) — crossing the bar two grid steps earlier than s2, three than s1.
- **Product-law upper bound 3/3-sure at BOTH long contexts**: product point 256 passes 0.981/0.986/0.990 (joining 8×'s 0.986/0.993/0.988 at 128) — k\* ≤ d·ctx/32 is a six-seed-verified deployment guarantee through 16×.
- **Selection importance +4.7/+3.4**: k=128 random 0.926 vs top-k 0.973; k=256 0.956 vs 0.990 — comparable to s2, far above s1's +1.7/+1.8; the 16× selection spread {1.7, 4.4, 4.7} at k=128 is three-fold (dilution strongly seed-dependent).
- **Concentration**: eff support 498.13 (s1 526.39, s2 472.50 — mid-family, spread ~11%); top-128 0.608, top-256 0.746; per-position 64.91/435.27/929.55 — the eff↔knee correlation again does NOT sort across three points (s1 highest-eff/highest-knee, s2 lowest-eff/middle-knee, s3 middle-eff/lowest-knee), NO bounded working set at 16×, three seeds.
- **Deployable at (d=4, ctx=2048)**: **≥8.0× guaranteed (3/3), 9.1× median, 12.8× best — the BEST-EVER reading** (beats 10.7× at 8× s2). Distribution {8.0, 9.1, 12.8} wider than 8×'s {8.0, 9.1, 10.7}.

### The 16× three-seed table
| seed | k\* | × product (256) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 (NET-45) | 256 | 1.000 |
| 2 (NET-46) | 224 | 0.875 |
| **3 (this round)** | **160** | **0.625** |

### All 8 barriers
(a) clean — four horns + the law's direct test stated before the run, measured 160 outside ALL horns, yet the distribution's median landed exactly on the law's predicted center (the round separates point-accuracy 0/4 from structural confirmation 1/1); (b) clean — three-seed 16× spread / widening low tail / median-stable center: none in the Catalog (698-pkg) or literature; (c) confronted — d=4 × ctx=2048 real causal word LM, 4097 vocab, held-out loss+acc, three seeds at the longest cell; (d) clean — held-out last-10%, data-free top-k; (e) the SUBSTANCE, sharpened — the 16× three-seed distribution complete; honest limits: the s3=160 read razor-thin (+0.0012), the 0.625 low tail is ONE of three seeds (a fourth decides s3-specific vs stable), the median law is 2 contexts × 3 seeds; (f) clean — same metrics/protocol, binom SE ≈ 0.11% acc (retained SE ≈ 0.007), the razor margin documented, k=512 recovers 1.000 / k=768 1.003 (loss Δ0.0016), monotone recovery, NO crash (ALL_DONE_NET48); (g) fair — full-attention reference + same 0.98 bar + random-k at same k (seed 12345): gaps +4.7/+3.4, positive, the {1.7–4.7} seed spread informative; (h) sharpened — the widened {8.0–12.8} deployment spread is the deployment-relevant uncertainty at the longest cell, guarantee end 3/3-sure.

### Next
**A fourth seed at ctx=2048** (the LOW-TAIL test — s4=160/192 → the 0.625 low tail is real, a stable 16× feature; s4 in {224,256} → it was s3-specific; ~4–5h — the highest-value open cell now); a fourth seed at ctx=1024 (refine {96,112,128}; low value); d=8 @ ctx=256 s0 corner; d=8 compression floor check; carry chain at scale (the frontier).

Now 48 network experiments. Assessment v48. Paper 92.
